practice_questions.text: Give two inferences you can make from a source about the impact of the First World War on Russia by early 1917. You should support each inference with a detail from the source.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail (for example, casualty figures, the bread ration falling to 280g, queues outside Petrograd bakeries, or the railway breakdown). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the war had broken not just the army but the home front’s ability to feed itself. [4]
Secure: Two inferences supported by detail. One may be more developed than the other. [3]
Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that paraphrases the source rather than inferring from it. [2]
Emerging: A single point that summarises rather than infers, or that is not anchored to a source detail. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why opposition to the Tsar had grown so dangerous by February 1917.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Tsarina Alexandra and Rasputin
• the impact of the First World War
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation that weighs at least three causes (e.g. military disaster, the Tsar taking command at Stavka in 1915, the Alexandra–Rasputin scandal, food and fuel shortages in Petrograd, peasant land hunger). Uses the stimulus and adds at least one cause from own knowledge. Reaches a clear judgement on the most important cause. Accurate use of period vocabulary — autocracy, Stavka, Duma, Okhrana — throughout. [10–12]
Secure: Several causes explained with relevant detail and at least one cause beyond the stimulus. Some attempt at weighing the causes against each other but the judgement may be implicit. [7–9]
Developing: Identifies and describes more than one cause but the explanation is uneven; the answer leans on the stimulus rather than adding own knowledge. [4–6]
Emerging: Lists features of Russia in 1917 without explaining why they amounted to growing opposition; little or no use of own knowledge beyond the stimulus. [1–3]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the importance of Rasputin in the collapse of the Romanov regime.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents Rasputin’s influence on policy as decisive; the other argues his actual power was small but the public scandal around him destroyed the dynasty’s legitimacy). Each side is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]
Secure: A clear difference identified and supported by detail from both interpretations, but one side is more thinly supported. [3]
Developing: A difference identified, supported by detail from only one interpretation, or by a vague reference. [2]
Emerging: Summarises one interpretation without setting it against the other; or describes both without naming the central difference. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the importance of Rasputin.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians used different evidence (court memoirs versus Okhrana police reports), wrote at different times, or had different purposes (a political biography of Alexandra versus a wider social history of the home front). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) but with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the main reason the Tsar lost public support by early 1917?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of Russia in early 1917 — war casualties, Stavka, the Putilov strikes, the Rasputin murder, the bread ration — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’ rather than ‘which is right’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on Russia in 1917 and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the First World War was the main reason for the collapse of the Romanov regime by 1917?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the 1.7m military deaths, Tannenberg and the Masurian Lakes, Nicholas’s 1915 move to Stavka, the Putilov strike, the Petrograd bread ration, Rodzianko’s warnings — to test whether the war was the decisive factor. Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (autocracy, Duma, Stavka, Okhrana). [16–20 + up to 4 SPaG]

Developing: Engages with both interpretations but unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [6–10 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge; no clear judgement. SPaG: frequent errors or no period vocabulary. [1–5 + 0–1 SPaG]

before.content_html:
Six Days that Brought Down a Dynasty

The February Revolution did not look like a revolution on its first morning. It looked like another bread queue. Yet between Thursday 23 February and Thursday 2 March 1917 (Old Style), the Romanov dynasty — which had ruled Russia for more than three centuries — fell apart in six days. Nicholas II was abdicating in a railway carriage at Pskov before most of the country knew that anything had begun. The speed of the collapse is the central historical puzzle of the February Revolution: why did three hundred years of autocratic rule end in less than a week?

Key Fact

February Revolution timeline (Old Style 1917): 23 February — International Women’s Day strikes; 25 February — general strike across Petrograd; 27 February — Petrograd garrison mutinies and the Petrograd Soviet is formed; 2 March — Nicholas II abdicates at Pskov.

23–25 February: The Strikes Spread

23 February (Old Style) was International Women’s Day. Around 90,000 women textile workers walked out of factories on the Vyborg side of Petrograd, marching for ‘Bread!’ The Putilov works had already been locked out two days earlier after wage talks broke down, throwing 30,000 men onto the streets. The two streams joined. By 25 February the strike had become general — about 240,000 workers, roughly half the city’s industrial workforce, were out, and slogans had moved from ‘Bread!’ to ‘Down with the Tsar!’ and ‘Down with the war!’

Crucially, this was not a Bolshevik-led rising. Lenin was in Switzerland and would later write that he had not expected to see another revolution in his lifetime. The leadership came from inside the factories — Mensheviks, Socialist Revolutionaries and unaffiliated militants — and from the streets themselves.

Students often collapse February and October into one event led by Lenin. They were two distinct revolutions eight months apart, with different leaders and different aims. In February the Bolsheviks were a minority faction in Petrograd; their senior figures, including Lenin and Zinoviev, were abroad. The rising was largely spontaneous, driven by women textile workers, Putilov machinists and factory committees, and shaped on the streets rather than from a single party headquarters.

26–27 February: The Garrison Refuses to Fire

Nicholas, at Stavka in Mogilev, telegraphed orders on 25 February to the city governor General Khabalov: stop the disorder by morning. On Sunday 26 February troops fired on protesters in Znamenskaya Square, killing about forty people. The order broke the regime, not the protest. That night and the next morning soldiers of the Volynsky Regiment, sickened by what they had been ordered to do, mutinied. The Pavlovsky and Litovsky regiments followed. By the evening of 27 February, around 66,000 soldiers of the Petrograd garrison had joined the protesters. They opened the Kresty prison, set fire to the law courts and seized the Arsenal.

The army loyalty Nicholas had counted on for three centuries had collapsed in 48 hours. The military reasons were specific: most of the Petrograd garrison were not professional soldiers but raw conscripts, often older reservists, kept in barracks rather than sent to the front. They had no appetite for shooting working women they recognised from their own neighbourhoods.

Two Bodies Step Into the Vacuum

On 27 February two rival authorities were forming in the same building — the Tauride Palace, home of the Duma. Liberal Duma deputies, refusing the Tsar’s order to disband, set up a Provisional Committee under Mikhail Rodzianko. In the next room, factory delegates and mutinous soldiers elected the Petrograd Soviet, modelled on the 1905 St Petersburg Soviet. The Soviet’s Executive Committee was dominated at first by Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries. The two bodies negotiated a deal: the Duma Committee would form a Provisional Government; the Soviet would not oppose it as long as the new government delivered civil liberties, an amnesty for political prisoners and democratic elections.

There was no popular vote to remove the Tsar. Nicholas was forced out by his own generals. On 1 March his train, trying to return from Stavka, was diverted to Pskov. There, his Chief of Staff General Mikhail Alekseev polled the front commanders by telegram. Every one of them — including the Tsar’s uncle, Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaevich — recommended abdication. They told him the army would not fight on for a regime that had lost the capital. It was a generals’ coup dressed up as a constitutional formality.

2 March: The Abdication

On the evening of 2 March 1917 (Old Style) Nicholas II signed his abdication in his railway carriage at Pskov. He abdicated not only for himself but also for his haemophiliac son Alexei, on the grounds that he could not bear to be parted from him; the throne therefore passed to his brother Grand Duke Michael. The next day Michael refused the crown unless a Constituent Assembly endorsed it — which it never did. Three centuries of Romanov rule ended without a coronation, in a railway siding, with no successor.

Key Fact

The Tsar fell in days, not months, because the Petrograd garrison’s mutiny on 27 February took away his last instrument of power and his own front commanders advised him to abdicate. Without the army, three centuries of autocracy had nothing left to stand on.

lessons.title: The October Revolution: The Bolshevik Seizure of Power

before.content_html:
A Coup, a Revolution, or Both?

By the autumn of 1917 the Provisional Government had run out of room. The army was disintegrating; peasants were seizing land in the countryside; food was running out in the cities. Into this vacuum stepped the Bolsheviks. On the night of 25–26 October 1917 (Old Style), a few thousand Red Guards, soldiers of the Petrograd garrison and Kronstadt sailors took control of the railway stations, the telegraph offices, the bridges and finally the Winter Palace itself. The Provisional Government was arrested without serious resistance. Most of Petrograd carried on as normal that night. The October Revolution was both a tightly planned seizure of power and the political punchline of a year in which the Bolsheviks had built genuine support in the city’s soviets and factories.

Key Fact

The Bolsheviks won in October because their opponents were exhausted, their slogans (‘Peace, Land, Bread’) answered the most urgent demands of the country, Trotsky organised the seizure through the Petrograd Soviet’s Military Revolutionary Committee, and Lenin pushed the party past its hesitations into action.

Lenin’s Return and the April Theses

In April 1917 Vladimir Lenin reached Petrograd in a sealed train provided by the German government, which had every reason to want a Russia out of the war. The same evening, at the Finland Station, he set out his April Theses. The programme stunned even his own party. There must be no support for the Provisional Government. There must be peace, immediately. The land must go to the peasants. The banks and the great factories must be brought under workers’ control. And, above all, ‘All Power to the Soviets’.

Senior Bolsheviks like Kamenev and Stalin had been edging towards conditional support for the Provisional Government. The April Theses ended that. Within weeks the Bolshevik Party had a single direction: opposition to the war and to the government, framed by the slogan that fitted on a banner — ‘Peace, Land, Bread’.

Students sometimes argue Lenin was a German agent because Berlin paid for the sealed train. The two interests aligned without one controlling the other. Germany wanted Russia out of the war and was happy to fund anyone who promised that. Lenin wanted to take a Russia he saw as ripe for revolution out of an imperialist war. Each used the other. The July Days ‘German agent’ leaks were politically devastating in the moment but historians since have shown there is no evidence Lenin took policy direction from Berlin. Strong answers note the funding without collapsing it into control.

The July Days — A Setback Lenin Survived

In early July 1917 Petrograd erupted. Kronstadt sailors and Petrograd soldiers, fearing a transfer to the front, demonstrated for ‘All Power to the Soviets’. The Bolsheviks dithered between leading the rising and trying to restrain it. Kerensky’s government accused Lenin of being a paid German agent and leaked documents in support. Pravda was shut, Trotsky and Kamenev were arrested, and Lenin fled across the Finnish border disguised as a railway worker. Bolshevik membership briefly fell. By August 1917 it looked, on paper, as if the radical left had been broken.

Sergei Eisenstein’s 1928 film ‘October’ staged a Petrograd-wide assault on the Winter Palace. The reality was small. The seizure of power was carried out by perhaps 15,000–20,000 Red Guards, soldiers and Kronstadt sailors organised by Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee. Most of the city carried on as normal that night — trams ran, theatres opened, restaurants served dinner. The Bolsheviks did, however, command real popular support: by September they held majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets and dominated the factory committees. Strong answers separate the small mechanics of the seizure from the broad political shift that made it possible.

Trotsky and the Military Revolutionary Committee

In September 1917 the Bolsheviks won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets. Lev Trotsky — a recent recruit to Bolshevism — was elected chair of the Petrograd Soviet. On 12 October the Soviet, on his proposal, set up the Military Revolutionary Committee (MRC), nominally to defend the city against any new Kornilov-style revolt. In practice the MRC was the planning headquarters of the October Revolution. It contacted the city’s garrison units, won pledges of loyalty, and decided which buildings would be seized first.

Lenin, in hiding in Finland, sent furious letters demanding that the party seize power before the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets opened. He returned to Petrograd in disguise on 10 October. That night, at a Bolshevik Central Committee meeting, the vote was ten in favour, two against, with Kamenev and Zinoviev opposing — both later leaked the decision to a Menshevik newspaper, which is one reason the rising had to happen quickly.

The Night of 25–26 October

From the early hours of 25 October (Old Style), MRC units took the railway stations, the State Bank, the Central Telegraph Office, the bridges and the General Staff building. Kerensky slipped out of Petrograd by car, supposedly to find loyal troops, and never returned to power. By late afternoon almost the entire city was under Bolshevik control except for the Winter Palace, where the remnants of the Provisional Government waited under the protection of cadets and the Women’s Battalion of Death. Around 9pm the cruiser Aurora, anchored on the Neva, fired a blank shell as a signal. The Winter Palace was rushed in the small hours of 26 October. The ministers were arrested in their cabinet room.

When the Second Congress of Soviets convened the same night, the Bolsheviks had a fait accompli to present. Lenin read out the ‘Decree on Peace’ and the ‘Decree on Land’: an immediate end to the war and the transfer of all gentry, Church and Crown estates to peasant communes. The Mensheviks and right-wing Socialist Revolutionaries walked out in protest. Trotsky famously sneered: ‘Go to where you belong — the dustbin of history.’

Key Fact

Trotsky organised the October seizure of power as chair of the Petrograd Soviet and head of the Military Revolutionary Committee; Lenin returned from hiding only days before, but he was the political will who pushed the party past its hesitations and authored the first decrees of the new Soviet government.

Why the Bolsheviks Won

Strong answers explain Bolshevik victory by combining two sets of reasons. The Provisional Government had collapsed under its own weight: the failed war, the postponed Constituent Assembly, the Kornilov Affair. The Bolsheviks then converted that vacuum through Lenin’s political programme, Trotsky’s organisational grip on the Petrograd Soviet, and slogans — Peace, Land, Bread — that addressed the things people actually wanted. The seizure on 25–26 October was small, but the political and military space it filled was real.

lessons.title: Early Bolshevik Decrees and the Constituent Assembly

before.content_html:
Power on Paper, Power in Practice

When the Second Congress of Soviets dispersed on 27 October 1917 (Old Style), the Bolsheviks had a capital, a cabinet and a stack of unsigned decrees. They did not yet have a country. Most of the old empire had not heard of the seizure; the bureaucracy refused to take orders; the railways stopped working; the army was disintegrating on the front. In the eight months between October 1917 and the execution of the Romanovs in July 1918, Lenin’s government tried to lock in its position with three weapons: a flood of headline-grabbing decrees, the closure of every rival institution, and the terror of the new secret police. This lesson tracks the first two. The Cheka comes later.

Key Fact

Between October and December 1917 the Bolsheviks issued four headline decrees: the Decree on Peace (immediate end to the war), the Decree on Land (gentry, Crown and Church estates to the peasants), the Decree on Workers’ Control (factory committees over the bosses) and the Decree on Nationalities (right of self-determination for non-Russian peoples). They were popular promises that Lenin’s government did not fully control.

Sovnarkom — A New Government in Twenty-Four Hours

On 26 October the Second Congress of Soviets ratified the formation of a new government, the Sovnarkom — the Council of People’s Commissars. Lenin became chairman. Trotsky took foreign affairs. Joseph Stalin was given the Commissariat for Nationalities. Anatoly Lunacharsky took education. Alexandra Kollontai became Commissar for Social Welfare — the first woman in a modern European cabinet. The Mensheviks and the right Socialist Revolutionaries had walked out of Congress in protest, so Sovnarkom was an entirely Bolshevik body.

Almost immediately the new government had to face a sabotage strike by the old civil service. Bank clerks refused to release funds. Foreign Ministry staff burned files. Telegraph operators cut off Petrograd. The Bolsheviks responded by sending Red Guards into ministries to break locks and physically force compliance. The new state was being built one office at a time.

The Decrees: Peace, Land, Workers’ Control, Nationalities

The Decree on Peace demanded an immediate armistice and a peace without annexations or indemnities. The Allies ignored it. Germany did not. Within weeks the new Russian government was at the negotiating table at Brest-Litovsk.

The Decree on Land transferred all gentry, Crown and Church estates to peasant communes without compensation. In practice, peasants had been seizing land themselves since the summer; the decree gave their action the legal stamp of the new government. The Bolsheviks knew the policy was lifted directly from the Socialist Revolutionaries’ programme, but Lenin took it anyway: at this stage the priority was to win peasant acceptance.

The Decree on Workers’ Control put factory committees in charge of monitoring the bosses, the books and production targets. It was not yet full nationalisation — private owners remained in place — but it shifted authority on the shop floor. The Decree on Workers’ Control was the most popular of the new measures in the cities.

The Decree on Nationalities, drafted by Stalin and Lenin, declared that all peoples of the former Russian empire had the right to self-determination, including secession. Within months Finland, Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic states had taken Bolshevik leaders at their word and declared independence. Bolshevik policy then quietly hardened: self-determination, in practice, would mean rule by local Bolsheviks.

Students often write that the Bolsheviks ‘nationalised everything’ in 1917. They did not. Workers’ Control was first, in November 1917, and only put committees over the bosses, not in place of them. The State Bank was nationalised in December 1917. Major industries followed in stages through 1918, but full nationalisation across the economy only arrived with War Communism in mid-1918, after the Civil War had begun. Strong answers separate the early decrees from the wartime emergency that followed them.

The Constituent Assembly — Elected and Dispersed

The Constituent Assembly elections of 12 November 1917 had been promised by every party in 1917, including the Bolsheviks, and Lenin let them go ahead. The result was inconvenient. The Socialist Revolutionaries took roughly 40 per cent of the vote, the Bolsheviks roughly 24 per cent, the Kadets and Mensheviks around 5 per cent each. The peasant majority of Russia had voted SR. Bolshevik strength was concentrated in Petrograd, Moscow and the army.

The Assembly opened in the Tauride Palace on 5 January 1918. The SR leader Viktor Chernov was elected chair. The Bolsheviks demanded the Assembly endorse Sovnarkom’s decrees as a condition for continuing. The Assembly refused. Lenin walked out. The next morning the Red Guard locked the doors. Yakov Sverdlov, the Bolshevik secretary of the Central Executive Committee, declared the Assembly dissolved. It had sat for less than a day.

Key Fact

The Bolsheviks came second in the only nationwide free election in 1917. The Socialist Revolutionaries won roughly 40 per cent against the Bolsheviks’ 24 per cent. Lenin closed the Assembly down on 6 January 1918 because, as he later argued, ‘a soviet republic is a higher form of democracy than the bourgeois Constituent Assembly’.

Banning the Opposition

The closure of the Assembly was the start of a wider clamp-down on rival parties. The Kadets had been outlawed in late November 1917 as ‘enemies of the people’. The Left Socialist Revolutionaries left Sovnarkom in March 1918 in protest at the Brest-Litovsk peace and were progressively shut out of the soviets. By the summer of 1918 the right SRs and Mensheviks had been banned from the soviets too. By 1921 the ban on factions inside the Bolshevik Party itself, agreed at the Tenth Party Congress, completed the picture: only one party, and only one line within it, would be tolerated. Strong answers trace the line from the closure of the Constituent Assembly to one-party rule rather than treating each step as separate.

The Romanovs at Ekaterinburg

Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated in March 1917 and been moved by the Provisional Government to Tobolsk in Siberia. After October the Bolsheviks transferred the family to the Ipatiev House in Ekaterinburg. As the Civil War approached the Urals in the summer of 1918, the local Bolshevik leadership, almost certainly with Moscow’s authorisation, decided to act. On the night of 16–17 July 1918 Nicholas, Alexandra, their five children and four servants were taken to a basement room and shot. There was no trial. The bodies were destroyed and hidden in mineshafts outside the town.

Students sometimes write that the Romanovs were tried before being executed. They were not. The shootings at the Ipatiev House were carried out without trial on direct orders from the Ural Regional Soviet, almost certainly authorised in Moscow. The reason given at the time was the approach of White and Czech Legion forces who might have rescued the Tsar; the deeper reason was that as long as the Romanovs lived they remained a focal point for monarchist resistance. With the family gone, the Whites had no candidate for the throne. The execution was also not announced honestly — only Nicholas was reported shot, and the deaths of Alexandra, the four daughters and the heir Alexei were denied by the regime for years.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918) cost Russia a quarter of its population, a quarter of its industry and almost half of its grain land — but Lenin treated the loss as the breathing space the new state needed to survive.
  • The Civil War of 1918–21 was fought between a unified Red regime in the centre and a coalition of separate White armies on the periphery, with limited foreign intervention from Britain, France, the United States and Japan.
  • The Reds won because they held the central railway hub, had unified leadership under Lenin and Sovnarkom, built a 5-million-strong Red Army under Trotsky, and used propaganda to brand the Whites as monarchists and foreign agents.
before.content_html:
A Peace That Saved the Revolution

By the time Russian and German negotiators sat down at Brest-Litovsk in December 1917, the Russian army had stopped fighting in any meaningful sense. Soldiers were walking home; trains were being commandeered to take them; officers had lost the authority to issue orders that would be obeyed. Lenin’s Decree on Peace had promised an immediate armistice. The Germans answered with terms that nobody in Russia wanted to sign. The peace that followed humiliated the new Soviet state, split the Bolshevik leadership and lit the fuse of a civil war that would kill millions. Within months Trotsky was building a new Red Army from scratch, the Whites were marching on Moscow and Petrograd, and foreign troops were landing on Russian soil.

Key Fact

The Reds won the Civil War of 1918–21 because they held the central railway hub of Russia (interior lines), they had unified leadership under Lenin and Sovnarkom while the Whites fought as separate armies, Trotsky built a 5-million-strong Red Army with conscription and ex-Tsarist officers, and Bolshevik propaganda framed the Reds as defenders of revolution and Russia against monarchist returnees and foreign invaders.

The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 1918

The German terms were brutal. Russia would lose Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Ukraine — roughly a quarter of its population, a quarter of its industry and almost half of its grain-producing land. Trotsky, who led the first Soviet delegation, tried a strategy he called ‘no war, no peace’ — refusing to sign while ordering full demobilisation. The Germans responded by simply marching deeper into Russia in February 1918. With nothing to stop them, Lenin overruled Trotsky and the ‘Left Communists’ in the Central Committee. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was signed on 3 March 1918.

Reactions were sharply divided. War-weary peasants and workers in the central provinces were relieved that the slaughter was over. The Left Socialist Revolutionaries, who had joined Sovnarkom in coalition, walked out in protest and within weeks had launched an uprising in Moscow. Inside the Bolshevik Party itself, Bukharin’s ‘Left Communists’ argued that signing was a betrayal of revolutionary internationalism. Lenin’s answer was pragmatic: a breathing space at any price was worth more than a doomed revolutionary war. By November 1918 Germany had collapsed and Sovnarkom annulled the treaty. The territorial losses, however, were the seed of the conflict that followed.

Students often write that the treaty was universally hated. It was not. Peasant villages that had lost sons at the front saw an end to the war as the most basic Bolshevik promise being kept. Sovnarkom kept producing pamphlets explaining that the breathing space would be used to consolidate revolutionary Russia. The treaty was a foundational grievance for the Whites and for foreign-intervention governments — but at home Lenin’s gamble that the country would tolerate the loss of Ukraine and the Baltics in exchange for peace was largely vindicated. Strong answers separate elite Bolshevik anger from war-weary popular relief.

The Whites and the Outbreak of Civil War

The opposition to Bolshevik rule was loose and incoherent. The Whites were not a single army but a label for several armies fighting in different theatres. General Anton Denikin led the Volunteer Army in the south. Admiral Alexander Kolchak set up a government at Omsk in Siberia and was recognised by other White leaders as ‘Supreme Ruler’. General Nikolai Yudenich attacked Petrograd from Estonia. General Pyotr Wrangel took over the southern army after Denikin and finally evacuated his troops from Crimea in November 1920.

The catalyst for full-scale war was the revolt of the Czech Legion in May 1918. Czech and Slovak prisoners of war from the Austro-Hungarian army, organised into a 40,000-strong unit on Bolshevik soil and trying to leave Russia by way of Vladivostok, fell out with local Soviet authorities and turned their rifles on the Bolsheviks. Within weeks they had seized stations along the Trans-Siberian Railway and helped a Socialist Revolutionary government, the Komuch, take Samara. The Bolsheviks now faced multiple fronts at once.

Trotsky and the Red Army

In March 1918 Lenin moved Trotsky from foreign affairs to war. As Commissar for War, Trotsky inherited an army that did not exist. The old Tsarist forces had dissolved; the Red Guards were factory militias of a few thousand. By the end of 1920 Trotsky had built a Red Army of around 5 million. He did it by reintroducing conscription, recruiting roughly 50,000 ex-Tsarist officers as ‘military specialists’ under the watch of political commissars, and reimposing harsh military discipline including the death penalty for desertion.

Trotsky’s armoured train was the symbol of the war effort. From it he travelled the fronts almost without stopping, rushed reserves to threatened sectors, addressed wavering units in person and shot deserters and corrupt commanders. Strong students note that this drive was matched by Lenin’s political grip in Moscow and the Cheka’s terror in the rear. Trotsky did not win the Civil War alone, but the Red Army he built was the indispensable instrument of victory.

Key Fact

By the end of 1920 Trotsky had built the Red Army to roughly 5 million troops. He used conscription, recruited around 50,000 ex-Tsarist officers as ‘military specialists’ under the watch of political commissars, and reimposed harsh discipline including the death penalty for desertion.

Foreign Intervention

From the spring of 1918 onwards British, French, American and Japanese forces landed at Russian ports. The British went into Murmansk and Archangel in the north and the Caucasus in the south. The French landed in Odessa. The Americans deployed troops in Vladivostok and the Russian north. Japan put around 70,000 men into the Russian Far East. The official aim was first to keep Allied war supplies out of German hands, and after November 1918 to strangle Bolshevism in its cradle. The reality was indecisive. Allied governments were exhausted by the world war and unable to commit large forces. By 1920 most foreign troops had withdrawn.

Bolshevik propaganda used the intervention as a gift. The Reds presented themselves as the defenders of Russia against foreign invaders propping up monarchist generals. Strong answers point out that the intervention may have prolonged the war but did relatively little militarily; politically it helped the Bolsheviks more than it hurt them.

Peasants disliked both sides. White armies seized grain and conscripted men just as harshly as the Reds did, and on the territory the Whites recovered they often returned land to the gentry — a fatal mistake in a country where the peasantry had just gained land under the Bolshevik decree. The Whites lost the Civil War mainly for structural reasons. They could not coordinate Denikin in the south, Kolchak in Siberia and Yudenich in the Baltic; they had no common political programme; they relied on monarchist symbols that alienated socialists; and the Reds held the central railway hub of Russia, while the Whites had to march in from the periphery. Strong answers separate ‘the Whites were unpopular’ from the harder, more accurate point about coordination and geography.

Why the Reds Won

Strong answers explain Red victory by combining four sets of reasons. First, geography: the Reds held Moscow, Petrograd and the central railway hub, giving them interior lines and short supply routes. Second, leadership: Lenin and Sovnarkom gave the Reds a single political authority while the Whites had no equivalent. Third, the Red Army: Trotsky’s mass conscript force, ex-Tsarist officers under commissar oversight, and ruthless discipline. Fourth, propaganda: the Reds offered land, peace and bread, and presented their opponents as monarchists and foreign agents. The Whites’ weaknesses — division, scattered fronts, the return of land to gentry — finished the case. By November 1920 Wrangel had evacuated Crimea, and the war was effectively over.

lessons.title: Red Terror, the Cheka and the Kronstadt Mutiny

before.content_html:
Survival by Terror

Bolshevik survival in 1918 owed as much to fear as to military victory. While Trotsky was building the Red Army at the front, a parallel apparatus was being built in the rear: the secret police, the Red Terror and the political discipline that turned a small revolutionary party into the only legal organisation in the country. By 1922 the Bolsheviks had a one-party state, a centralised dictatorship of the Politburo, a new federal Union of Soviet Socialist Republics — and a profound problem: their own base in the navy and the working class had begun to turn on them. The Kronstadt Mutiny of March 1921 was the moment that forced Lenin to rethink what Bolshevism in power could afford to do.

Key Fact

The Red Terror was launched in September 1918 after Fanny Kaplan’s assassination attempt on Lenin and the murder of the Petrograd Cheka boss Uritsky. It was carried out by the Cheka under Felix Dzerzhinsky and targeted Whites, the bourgeoisie, clergy, the Kadets and any group judged a threat to the revolution. Estimates run from 50,000 to over 100,000 killed by 1922.

The Founding of the Cheka

On 7 December 1917 Sovnarkom set up the Cheka — the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage. Its first chairman was Felix Dzerzhinsky, a Polish-born Bolshevik who had spent years in Tsarist prisons. The original brief was narrow: investigate sabotage in the new ministries, suppress speculation, and confront counter-revolutionary plots. The brief did not stay narrow. By the summer of 1918 the Cheka was operating in every province, conducting summary arrests, running its own prisons and shooting people without trial.

Dzerzhinsky himself argued the Cheka was an instrument of class war, not of justice. ‘We stand for organised terror — this should be frankly admitted,’ he said in July 1918. The body operated outside the courts; its decisions could not be appealed; the death sentence was its standard penalty. By 1921 it employed roughly 250,000 staff and informants.

The Red Terror, August–September 1918

On 30 August 1918 the head of the Petrograd Cheka, Moisei Uritsky, was assassinated by a young military cadet. The same evening Fanny Kaplan, a Socialist Revolutionary, shot Lenin twice as he left a Moscow factory meeting. Lenin survived but was seriously wounded. Sovnarkom responded with a formal Decree on the Red Terror on 5 September 1918, authorising mass arrests, hostage-taking and summary execution.

In Petrograd alone perhaps 800 hostages were shot in the first weeks. Across the country the Cheka took thousands of class enemies, clergy, Kadets and former Tsarist officials and shot them in batches. Forced labour camps for political prisoners were set up. The intent was deliberately public: terror was meant to deter not just plots, but the social classes from which plots might come. Strong answers note that this was different from the Civil War battlefield killing — the Red Terror was a political weapon used in the Bolsheviks’ own rear.

Students often treat the Soviet secret police as a single unchanging organisation. They were not. The Cheka (1917–22) was Lenin’s wartime instrument under Dzerzhinsky. It was renamed and restructured into the GPU in 1922, then the OGPU in 1923, before becoming the NKVD under Yagoda in 1934. Yezhov ran the NKVD during the Great Terror of 1936–38; Beria took over in 1938. The continuity was institutional — secret police, summary arrests, terror — but the specific organisation, leadership and scale changed dramatically. Strong answers name the body of the right decade.

Centralisation: Politburo, USSR, Ban on Factions

Bolshevik power was concentrated as fast as opposition was crushed. In March 1919 the Eighth Party Congress created the Politburo — a small inner cabinet of around five members — and the Orgburo, to handle party appointments. Real decision-making moved from the open Party Congress to the closed Politburo. In 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary of the Party, an apparently dull job that gave him control over thousands of party appointments.

In December 1922 the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, the Ukrainian SSR, the Belorussian SSR and the Transcaucasian SSR were federated into the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. On paper the new state recognised national difference and the right of secession. In practice it was governed by a single Communist Party of the Soviet Union with its centre in Moscow. The Tenth Party Congress of March 1921 had already taken the third decisive step: a ban on factions inside the party itself, agreed even as the Civil War was ending. Bolshevism was now one party with one line.

Key Fact

Bolshevik centralisation between 1919 and 1922 produced three decisive moves: the Politburo as a closed inner cabinet (March 1919), the ban on factions inside the party at the Tenth Party Congress (March 1921), and the formal establishment of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (30 December 1922). Together they made the regime a one-party dictatorship of the Politburo.

The Kronstadt Mutiny, March 1921

The sailors of the Kronstadt naval base on an island near Petrograd had been the ‘pride and glory of the revolution’. They had stormed the Winter Palace in 1917 and helped defend the Bolshevik regime. By the winter of 1920–21 their faith was gone. The grain requisitioning policies of War Communism had pushed peasant relatives to the edge of starvation; strikes were spreading in Petrograd; food rations had been cut again.

On 28 February 1921 the crew of the battleship Petropavlovsk, led by Stepan Petrichenko, issued a fifteen-point resolution. They demanded fresh elections to the soviets by secret ballot, freedom of speech and press for socialist parties, the release of political prisoners, an end to grain requisitioning, and the right of peasants to farm freely. The slogan was devastating: ‘Soviets without Bolsheviks’. By 7 March some 16,000 sailors and soldiers had joined the revolt.

Trotsky and Tukhachevsky led the Red Army assault. The first attack across the ice on 7 March failed. The second, on 17 March, broke through; an estimated 10,000 Red soldiers and 1,000 sailors were killed in the fighting, and several thousand mutineers were shot or sent to camps after the surrender. Petrichenko escaped to Finland.

Soviet propaganda after 1921 painted the mutineers as White-led counter-revolutionaries. They were not. The Kronstadt sailors had been the ‘pride and glory’ of October 1917. Their resolution called for a return to the original 1917 promise — free soviets, free press for socialist parties, the right of peasants to farm freely. The shock of Kronstadt was precisely that it came from the Bolshevik base. Strong answers note that this is what gave the revolt its political weight: when sailors who had carried the revolution turned against it, the regime had to listen.

Why Kronstadt Forced a Rethink

Kronstadt opened on 1 March 1921. The Tenth Party Congress opened in Moscow a week later, on 8 March, while the assault was being prepared. By the time it closed on 16 March the Congress had agreed two huge changes. It had banned all factions inside the party — closing off internal opposition just as the regime was crushing external opposition by force. And it had launched the New Economic Policy, ending grain requisitioning and authorising small private trade. The two decisions look contradictory. Politically they were two sides of the same answer to Kronstadt: tighten the party, but loosen the grip on the peasantry. Lenin admitted the regime had ‘come within a hair’s breadth of disaster’. Strong answers connect Kronstadt directly to the NEP, not as separate events but as cause and consequence.

lessons.title: War Communism, the NEP and Society Under Lenin

before.content_html:
Two Economies in Three Years

In a span of three years between 1918 and 1921 the Bolsheviks ran two completely different economies. The first, War Communism, was a wartime emergency that nationalised industry, banned private trade and seized grain at gunpoint. The second, the New Economic Policy, was a partial retreat to the market that allowed peasants to keep their surplus and small workshops to operate for profit. Lenin called the NEP a ‘temporary tactical retreat’. Behind both lay the same political question: how could a Bolshevik regime committed to socialism govern a country whose population was 80 per cent peasant and overwhelmingly hostile to its grain policy? Alongside these economic shifts, Lenin’s government carried out radical social reforms in marriage, education and religion that reshaped daily life for Soviet women, children and the Orthodox Church.

Key Fact

War Communism (1918–21) imposed grain requisitioning, full nationalisation of industry, a ban on private trade and labour conscription. The New Economic Policy (March 1921) replaced grain requisitioning with a tax in kind, allowed small private trade and small private workshops, and kept the ‘commanding heights’ (heavy industry, banks, foreign trade, transport) under state control. Lenin replaced the first with the second after the Kronstadt Mutiny and the 1921 famine made further peasant revolt the regime’s greatest danger.

War Communism, 1918–21

When the Civil War began in the summer of 1918, Bolshevik-held territory was cut off from Ukraine’s grain. Sovnarkom responded with War Communism. Armed grain detachments were sent into the villages to requisition surplus food. All factories with more than ten workers were nationalised by June 1918, and almost all private trade was banned. Wages became part-cash, part-rations of bread and goods. Workers were conscripted into labour duties as if into the army; transport, fuel and food distribution all came under direct state control.

Strong students see War Communism as both ideology and emergency. The hardline left of the party welcomed it as a leap into socialism. Lenin himself, more cautiously, presented it as the means by which a besieged Soviet state could feed the Red Army and the cities. Either reading was tested in late 1920. The cities had emptied: Petrograd’s population had fallen from 2.4 million in 1917 to about 750,000 by 1920. Industrial output stood at roughly 20 per cent of its 1913 level. Peasants had stopped sowing more grain than they needed because the surplus would simply be taken.

The 1921 Famine

The collapse of grain production met two bad seasons in a row. The harvests of 1920 and 1921 failed across the Volga region. Peasants who had eaten their seed grain to survive the winter had nothing to plant. Cannibalism was reported in the worst-affected villages. Estimates of deaths run to around five million. The Bolsheviks accepted aid from the American Relief Administration under Herbert Hoover, who fed perhaps 10 million people at the peak of operations. The famine destroyed any remaining argument that War Communism could be sustained politically.

Students often write that War Communism was abandoned because it didn’t work. Lenin’s own argument at the Tenth Party Congress in March 1921 was sharper than that. He admitted that the regime had ‘come within a hair’s breadth of disaster’ — the political danger of further peasant revolt, after Kronstadt and the Tambov rising, was now greater than any economic objection to retreat. The famine, the strikes in Petrograd, the Tambov peasant war and Kronstadt all pushed the same direction: concession to the peasantry was now a political necessity. Strong answers explain the abandonment as politically driven, not economically inevitable.

The New Economic Policy, March 1921

At the Tenth Party Congress in March 1921 Lenin announced the New Economic Policy. Grain requisitioning was replaced with a tax in kind: peasants paid a fixed share of their harvest in grain and could sell the rest on the open market. Small workshops employing fewer than twenty workers were returned to private ownership; small private trade was legalised. The state, however, kept the ‘commanding heights’ — banks, foreign trade, large factories and transport.

Reactions varied. War-weary peasants were relieved; food production recovered quickly and by 1925 grain output approached pre-war levels. Petty traders nicknamed ‘Nepmen’ appeared in the cities, opening shops, restaurants and workshops. Bukharin defended the NEP as a long-term road towards socialism via the peasantry. Hardline Bolsheviks — the ‘Left Communists’ — were appalled. Trotsky later attacked the NEP as a betrayal of revolution. Inside the party, the policy was the great economic divide of the 1920s, and would frame the succession struggle after Lenin’s death.

Students often describe the NEP as a return to capitalism. It was not. The state retained the ‘commanding heights’ — heavy industry, banks, transport and foreign trade. What was privatised was retail, small workshops and the peasant grain market. Lenin himself called the NEP ‘state capitalism’ and a ‘temporary tactical retreat’. By 1924 around three-quarters of retail trade was in private hands, but more than 80 per cent of industrial output remained in state factories. Strong answers separate the partial retreat in agriculture and small trade from the continuing state grip on heavy industry.

Key Fact

Under the New Economic Policy from March 1921, peasants paid a fixed tax in kind (a share of the harvest) and could sell the rest on the open market. Small private workshops and trade were legalised. The state kept the ‘commanding heights’ — heavy industry, banks, foreign trade and transport. Small private traders, the ‘Nepmen’, returned to the cities.

Women, Family and Education

Bolshevik social policy in the early 1920s was extraordinarily radical for its time. Marriage was made a civil registration; divorce became a postcard formality (the ‘postcard divorce’) requiring only one partner’s notification. In 1920 Soviet Russia became the first European country to legalise abortion on demand. Women gained equal pay in law, the vote, and the right to property and education. Alexandra Kollontai, as Commissar for Social Welfare, drove much of this legislation and pressed for state-funded maternity leave, communal kitchens and nurseries to release women from domestic labour into industrial work.

Education was reorganised under Anatoly Lunacharsky, the Commissar for Enlightenment. Schooling became free, secular and co-educational. Mass literacy campaigns — the Likbez — aimed to abolish illiteracy among adults. Roughly 5 million adults were enrolled in literacy classes by 1925. Religious teaching was banned in schools. Strong answers note the gap between sweeping legislation and slow rural reality: in many villages the new family law took a decade to bite, and the more radical experiments — such as communal living — were always urban and minority.

Religion, Culture and the Limits of Liberation

The Russian Orthodox Church was the regime’s major ideological rival. Church and state were formally separated in January 1918; Church land was nationalised, religious education in schools was abolished, and clergy lost the vote and ration cards. During the 1921–22 famine the regime confiscated Church valuables, ostensibly for famine relief, killing perhaps 8,000 clergy and lay believers in the operation. The League of the Militant Godless, founded in 1925, ran anti-religious propaganda and museums of atheism. Many of the early radical experiments — especially around the family — would be partially rolled back under Stalin in the 1930s, when divorce became harder, abortion was restricted, and traditional family roles were reinstated as Soviet ideals.

before.content_html:
A Succession Nobody Predicted

When Lenin died on 21 January 1924, almost no one inside the party expected Joseph Stalin to succeed him. Stalin held the dry administrative post of General Secretary, taken in April 1922 because no one else wanted it. The bigger names in the Politburo were Leon Trotsky, the architect of the October seizure of power and the Civil War victor; Lev Kamenev, head of the Moscow party; Grigory Zinoviev, head of the Leningrad party and chair of the Comintern; and Nikolai Bukharin, the leading party theorist and editor of Pravda. By January 1929 Trotsky was on a steamer to exile, Kamenev and Zinoviev had been expelled, and Bukharin had been broken. The General Secretary controlled the party.

Key Fact

Stalin defeated his rivals in three stages between 1924 and 1929: with Kamenev and Zinoviev he beat Trotsky’s Left Opposition (1925); with Bukharin and the right he beat Kamenev and Zinoviev’s United Opposition (1926–27); then he turned on Bukharin and the Right Opposition (1928–29). Trotsky was expelled from the party in 1927 and exiled from the USSR in January 1929.

Lenin’s Testament and the Funeral

In December 1922 and January 1923 Lenin dictated a series of notes that became known as his Testament. He warned the Central Committee that Stalin had ‘concentrated unlimited authority in his hands’ and added a postscript recommending that the party ‘remove Stalin from that position’. He criticised Trotsky for ‘excessive self-confidence’, accused Kamenev and Zinoviev of cowardice during October 1917, and called Bukharin a ‘valuable theoretician’ whose Marxism was incomplete. Lenin’s widow, Nadezhda Krupskaya, brought the document to the Politburo in May 1924. Kamenev and Zinoviev, frightened of Trotsky, persuaded the Central Committee to suppress it. Stalin offered to resign as General Secretary; the offer was rejected. The Testament was not read to the wider party.

Stalin then exploited the symbolism of Lenin’s funeral. He delivered a public oath to continue Lenin’s work and orchestrated a state ceremony that placed himself at the centre of the mourning. Trotsky, recovering from illness in the south, was told by Stalin that the funeral would take place a day earlier than it actually did, and so missed it altogether. Whether Stalin lied deliberately is contested, but the political cost to Trotsky was real: he was absent at the moment when Bolshevik authority was being publicly transferred. Through 1924 Stalin pushed the ‘Lenin cult’: the embalming of the body, the Lenin Mausoleum, the renaming of Petrograd to Leningrad, and quotation of Lenin in every speech. Each Stalin speech now opened with a Leninist text. The man who could quote Lenin most accurately could most easily claim to be his heir.

Students often write that Stalin was Lenin’s natural heir. The opposite is true. Lenin’s Testament explicitly recommended Stalin’s removal as General Secretary, and his postscript called Stalin ‘too rude’ for the role. The reason this misconception sticks is that Soviet propaganda from the 1930s onwards rewrote the 1920s as a smooth handover. Strong answers separate what Lenin actually wrote from what the regime later claimed, and credit Kamenev and Zinoviev’s 1924 decision to suppress the Testament as a turning point in the succession.

Stalin’s Strengths and His Rivals’ Weaknesses

Stalin’s real weapon was the General Secretaryship itself. The post controlled party appointments, congress agendas and membership records. Through the 1924 ‘Lenin Enrolment’ some 240,000 new members were admitted to the party — many young, working-class and personally loyal to the apparatus that had recruited them. Stalin used this power to pack delegations to party congresses with his supporters, ensuring votes went his way. He spoke a plain Russian that the new mass party understood, and he carefully avoided the polished theoretical style that made Trotsky and Bukharin sound like intellectuals lecturing the rank and file.

Trotsky’s strengths cut against him. His record in the Civil War as the founder of the Red Army gave him military prestige — but inside the Politburo this prestige read as Bonapartism, the danger that a charismatic general would replace the party with a personal dictatorship. He had only joined the Bolsheviks in August 1917; many old Bolsheviks remembered him as a Menshevik in the years before. He was a brilliant orator but a poor coalition-builder, often arrogant in committee, often absent from the party machine. Kamenev and Zinoviev had old credibility from the underground years but had been damaged by their public opposition to the October seizure of power. Bukharin, the most popular figure with the party’s younger generation, was a theorist rather than a manager, and his closeness to the NEP would prove fatal once Stalin turned against the policy.

Defeating the Left: Trotsky, 1923–25

The first phase of the succession was the Triumvirate — Stalin, Kamenev and Zinoviev — against Trotsky. The decisive ideological clash was over the future of the revolution. Trotsky argued for ‘Permanent Revolution’: Soviet Russia could not survive alone, and the regime had to push for revolution abroad, especially in industrialised Germany. Stalin and Bukharin replied with Socialism in One Country: with foreign revolutions clearly failing, the USSR had to build socialism inside its own borders. The Stalin–Bukharin position was practical, patriotic and reassuring; Trotsky’s sounded utopian and risky. At the Thirteenth Party Congress in May 1924 Trotsky was outvoted; in January 1925 he was forced to resign as Commissar for War.

Defeating the United Opposition, 1926–27

Once Trotsky was beaten, Stalin turned on his Triumvirate partners. Kamenev and Zinoviev, alarmed by the rising power of the General Secretariat and worried that the NEP was producing rural inequality, broke with Stalin in 1925 and proposed faster industrialisation. In 1926 they joined Trotsky to form the United Opposition. Stalin, allied now with Bukharin and the right of the party, used his control of party machinery to outvote and outmanoeuvre them. In November 1927 Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled from the Communist Party. In January 1928 Trotsky was deported to Alma-Ata in Kazakhstan; in January 1929 he was expelled from the USSR altogether.

Students often present 1924–28 as a debate about Permanent Revolution versus Socialism in One Country, decided on the merits. The argument mattered, but the votes did not turn on it. Stalin’s grip on the General Secretariat let him control who attended the congresses that took the decisions. The historian Stephen Kotkin has stressed that Stalin’s dullness was strategic: every rival underestimated him because he sounded like a clerk. Strong answers explain that ideology framed the conflict but the party machine decided the outcome.

Defeating the Right: Bukharin, 1928–29

The third phase reversed the first. The 1927–28 grain procurement crisis — peasants withholding grain because state prices were too low — pushed Stalin towards forced collectivisation and rapid industrialisation. Bukharin, the architect of the NEP, called this an attack on the alliance with the peasantry and warned in 1928 of ‘military-feudal exploitation’ of the countryside. Stalin manoeuvred against him exactly as he had against the others: packing committees, controlling agendas, denouncing the ‘Right Opposition’ as enemies of socialism. By April 1929 Bukharin was removed from the Politburo. By the end of 1929 — ‘the year of the great breakthrough’ — Stalin’s 50th birthday was being celebrated as a national event, the cult of personality had begun, and the General Secretary was the undisputed leader of the USSR.

Key Fact

The succession was decided in three rounds: 1923–25 Stalin, Kamenev and Zinoviev (the Triumvirate) defeated Trotsky’s Left Opposition; 1926–27 Stalin and Bukharin defeated the United Opposition (Trotsky, Kamenev, Zinoviev); 1928–29 Stalin defeated Bukharin’s Right Opposition. Each round used the same weapon — control of party appointments through the General Secretariat.

lessons.title: Collectivisation and the Attack on the Kulaks

before.content_html:
Why Stalin Abandoned the NEP

By 1927 the New Economic Policy had restored Soviet grain output to roughly the level of 1913. But the cities were growing faster than the countryside could feed them, and the state could not industrialise on a peasant economy that sold its surplus on an open market. Then came the 1927–28 grain procurement crisis. Faced with low state prices, peasants in the major grain regions withheld grain rather than sell it cheap, and state purchases ran perhaps 25 per cent below what was needed. Stalin travelled to Siberia in January 1928 and ordered local officials to seize grain by force in the manner of War Communism. By the end of 1929 he had committed the regime to a complete reversal of the NEP: the wholesale collectivisation of agriculture and the ‘liquidation of the kulaks as a class’.

Key Fact

Stalin’s aims for collectivisation were threefold: feed the cities reliably, fund industrialisation by exporting grain, and break peasant resistance to Bolshevik rule. Peasants were to be moved off their family plots into kolkhozes (collective farms) and sovkhozes (state farms). Mechanisation came through state-run Machine Tractor Stations, which doubled as political surveillance posts.

The First Wave, 1929–30

In December 1929 Stalin announced collectivisation. The plan was to push 25 per cent of peasant households into collectives by the autumn of 1930; in many regions local officials, terrified of failure, drove the figure far higher. By March 1930 around 58 per cent of peasant households had been collectivised, often by armed party teams (the ‘25,000-ers’ — urban communists sent into the villages) using threats, beatings and arrest. Peasants were ordered to bring all their land, livestock and tools to the new collective. Many slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them: between 1929 and 1933 the USSR lost roughly half its horses, more than 40 per cent of its cattle, and around two-thirds of its sheep and goats. Soviet livestock numbers did not recover until the 1950s.

In March 1930, with rural revolt threatening the spring sowing, Stalin published ‘Dizzy with Success’ in Pravda. He blamed local officials for excesses and allowed peasants to leave the new collectives. Within months perhaps half of those collectivised had walked out. The retreat was tactical. By the end of 1931 the campaign was renewed; by 1934 around 70 per cent of households were on collectives, and by 1937 the figure was over 90 per cent.

Dekulakisation

Stalin needed an enemy to drive collectivisation forward. The chosen target was the kulak, supposedly the wealthier peasant who hired labour and exploited his neighbours. In practice the term was applied flexibly to anyone who resisted — a peasant with one cow, a single hired hand, or a literate peasant who answered back. Local officials were given quotas of kulak families to identify, and the quotas expanded as the campaign rolled on. In January 1930 the Politburo divided kulaks into three categories: the first to be shot or sent to labour camps; the second to be deported to Siberia, the Urals or Kazakhstan; the third to be expelled from their villages and resettled on poor land. Around 1.8 million peasants were deported as ‘dekulakised’ between 1930 and 1932; perhaps 30,000 were executed in the first wave, and many more died in the resettlements from cold, hunger and disease.

Students often write that kulaks were a real class of wealthy peasants who exploited their neighbours. The Bolshevik category was always loose. By 1929 the Soviet countryside had been levelled by a decade of war, requisitioning and the redistribution of estate land in 1917; few peasants owned more than a small plot. The Royal Historical Society’s survey of Soviet rural history notes that the ‘kulak’ label was effectively a quota imposed from above and filled locally with whoever was resisting. The historian Lynne Viola has shown that ‘dekulakisation’ targeted middle peasants, women, the elderly and clergy as readily as wealthier farmers. Strong answers separate the propaganda category from the social reality.

The Holodomor, 1932–33

The grain quotas set by Moscow rose every year while output fell. In Ukraine and the North Caucasus the harvest of 1932 was poor; the quota set on the kolkhozes was higher than the villages could deliver and still feed themselves. Brigades of officials seized seed grain, hidden stocks and the reserve from peasant homes. In late 1932 a series of decrees made it a criminal offence to leave a famine zone, blacklisted villages from receiving manufactured goods, and barred peasants from migrating to the cities without internal passports. Grain continued to be exported from Soviet ports while villagers starved. The death toll from the resulting Holodomor — literally ‘death by hunger’ in Ukrainian — is estimated at around 3.5 to 5 million in Ukraine alone, with comparable death rates in Kazakhstan from the parallel collectivisation of nomadic herders.

Historians disagree on whether the Ukrainian famine was a deliberate national genocide. Robert Conquest and Anne Applebaum argue that Stalin used the famine as a weapon against Ukrainian national identity, citing the export of grain during the famine, the closure of borders, and the simultaneous attack on Ukrainian language, culture and Communist Party cadres. R. W. Davies and Stephen Wheatcroft argue for criminal indifference rather than directed national targeting — that Stalin was prepared to let the peasantry starve to fund industrialisation rather than singling out Ukrainians as a nation. Strong answers acknowledge that grain export, the blacklists and the internal-passport decree are agreed on; what is contested is the question of intent.

Successes and Failures

By 1937 over 90 per cent of peasant households were on collectives. The state now controlled grain procurement directly: it took what it needed from the farms before the peasantry got their share. Soviet grain exports paid for the foreign machinery imported under the First Five-Year Plan. The peasantry, the regime’s main political problem since 1917, had been broken as an independent force. From the regime’s viewpoint these were successes.

The cost was extraordinary. Soviet livestock losses were not made good for two decades. Grain output stagnated through the 1930s; per capita food consumption was lower in 1937 than in 1928. Several million people died in the famine. The dekulakised population, swept off into special settlements and labour camps, became one source of forced labour for the new factories and canals. Vyacheslav Molotov, chair of Sovnarkom, signed off the rising quotas; Lazar Kaganovich oversaw the Ukrainian operation in person. The political verdict on collectivisation depends on what is being weighed: state control of the countryside and grain for industry on one side, demographic catastrophe and a peasantry alienated for a generation on the other.

Key Fact

Roughly 1.8 million peasants were deported as ‘dekulakised’ between 1930 and 1932. The USSR lost about half its horses, 40 per cent of its cattle and two-thirds of its sheep and goats by 1933. Around 3.5 to 5 million people died in the Ukrainian famine of 1932–33, with further mass deaths in Kazakhstan. By 1937 over 90 per cent of peasant households were on collective farms.

lessons.title: The Five-Year Plans and Soviet Industry

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stalin’s four reasons for rapid industrialisation were defence against capitalist powers, autarky, the ideological need for an industrial working class, and victory over Bukharin’s Right Opposition. The First Five-Year Plan launched in October 1928 with targets set by Gosplan and enforced through the Commissariats and the secret police.
  • The First Plan (1928–32) built Magnitogorsk, the Dnieper Dam and the Belomor Canal, doubled coal output and quadrupled pig iron output on official figures — but real wages fell, Gulag labour built the showpieces, internal passports and labour-discipline laws bound workers to their factories, and 10,000 foreign engineers trained Soviet replacements.
  • The Second Plan (1933–37) promised consumer goods but delivered rearmament after 1935; the Stakhanovite movement from August 1935 turned a stage-managed coal record into a national propaganda lever to raise norms. The Third Plan (1938–41) was cut short by the German invasion, but the new industrial base east of the Urals carried the Soviet war effort.
before.content_html:
Why Stalin Chose Rapid Industrialisation

In November 1927 Stalin warned the Party Congress that ‘we are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must make good this distance in ten years. Either we do it, or they crush us.’ The argument rested on four reasons. First, defence: a peasant economy could not arm itself against the industrial powers of Europe and Japan. Second, autarky: an isolated socialist state needed to make at home what capitalist countries would not sell on credit. Third, ideology: socialism, in Marxist theory, required an industrial working class, and the USSR in 1928 was overwhelmingly rural. Fourth, succession: by tearing up the New Economic Policy, Stalin defined himself against Bukharin’s Right Opposition and seized the political initiative inside the party. The result was the First Five-Year Plan, launched in October 1928 with targets backdated to begin from 1 October 1928 and a one-year acceleration of the deadline announced in 1930.

Key Fact

Three Five-Year Plans framed Soviet industrialisation: the First (1928–32) prioritised heavy industry — coal, iron, steel, oil; the Second (1933–37) promised consumer goods but delivered defence and rearmament; the Third (1938–41) focused on armaments and was cut short by Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. Targets were set by Gosplan, the State Planning Commission, and enforced through the People’s Commissariats and the secret police.

Gosplan and the Planning System

Soviet planning was not what it claimed to be. Gosplan in Moscow set headline output figures for each sector. The Commissariats translated those into factory quotas. Local managers, on pain of arrest, had to fulfil — and ideally over-fulfil — the quota by the deadline. Inputs (coal, steel, labour, machinery) were allocated centrally rather than purchased on a market. Prices on planning targets were political, not economic. Managers responded by hoarding raw materials, padding workforce numbers, ignoring quality and faking returns. Targets in tonnes encouraged heavy, low-quality output: shoes the wrong sizes, nails the wrong weights, cement that did not set. Output figures published in Pravda as ‘over-fulfilment’ were inflated as a matter of political requirement, not as a neutral observation.

Students often quote Soviet headline figures — coal up four-fold, steel up four-fold — as if they were neutral measurements. They were not. Output was measured in inconsistent units across sectors, padded by managers desperate to fulfil quotas, and political over-fulfilment was a survival tactic during the Terror. The historian R. W. Davies, working with archival data, has shown that some sectors fell well short of plan and that consumer goods consistently lagged. Strong answers acknowledge that Soviet industry genuinely grew at remarkable speed — but treat the published figures as evidence of state ambition, not as exact fact.

The First Five-Year Plan, 1928–32

The First Plan poured everything into heavy industry. Coal, iron, steel, oil, electricity and machine tools were the priority; consumer goods, housing and food were starved. The flagship project was Magnitogorsk in the southern Urals, a steel city built from scratch around the iron ore of the Magnetic Mountain. The Dnieper hydroelectric dam was completed in 1932, then the largest in Europe. The Stalingrad and Kharkov tractor factories, the Moscow Metro (begun 1932), and the White Sea–Baltic Canal — the infamous Belomor Canal, dug largely by Gulag prisoners between 1931 and 1933 with around 12,000–25,000 dead — were among the headline projects. Coal output rose from around 36 million tonnes in 1928 to roughly 64 million in 1932; pig iron, steel and electricity all grew sharply. By 1932 the Plan was declared completed in four years and three months.

Workers paid for the speed. Real wages fell by perhaps half between 1928 and 1932 as food prices rose and consumer goods disappeared from the shops. Internal passports were introduced in December 1932 to stop workers leaving badly-supplied factories. Labour discipline laws criminalised lateness and absenteeism: from 1932 a single day’s unauthorised absence could cost a worker their job, ration card and accommodation. Foreign engineers — perhaps 10,000 of them, mostly American — were hired to install machinery, train Soviet workers and run the new plants until Soviet engineers could replace them.

The Second Five-Year Plan, 1933–37

The Second Plan was originally branded the ‘Three Goods’ Plan: better food, clothing and housing for Soviet citizens after the headlong drive of the First Plan. From 1933 to 1935 there was indeed some recovery in living standards: ration cards were abolished in 1935 and bread came back into the shops. From 1935, however, the international situation darkened with the rise of Nazi Germany. Defence spending rose from around 4 per cent of state expenditure in 1933 to over 16 per cent by 1937. The promised consumer goods were quietly dropped in favour of tanks, aircraft and shells. New industrial regions were developed in the Urals, Siberia and Kazakhstan, deliberately east of the Ural mountains so that German bombers could not reach them. The Moscow Metro opened its first line in 1935, hailed as a propaganda triumph by Lazar Kaganovich.

The Stakhanovite Movement

In August 1935 a Donbas miner called Alexei Stakhanov reportedly cut 102 tonnes of coal in a single six-hour shift — fourteen times the normal quota. Soviet propaganda turned him into a national hero. Workers who beat their norms were named Stakhanovites, given medals, bonuses, holidays in the Crimea and articles in Pravda. The movement was quickly used as a political lever: production norms were raised across whole industries on the basis of what the ‘hero’ had achieved. Stakhanov’s record itself had been carefully stage-managed — a team of helpers cleared the rubble, fitted the props and moved the coal — but the propaganda effect was real. Stakhanovites were resented on the shop floor by ordinary workers whose output expectations rose without a corresponding rise in pay.

Students often write that the Five-Year Plans raised living standards. The reality was more uneven. Real wages fell sharply during the First Plan; bread was rationed until 1935; housing in the new industrial cities was overcrowded and primitive. Working-class families gained free education, free healthcare, free childcare and the chance of upward mobility into engineering or managerial posts — the historian Sheila Fitzpatrick has stressed this generational mobility as a real social gain. But take-home pay only began to recover slowly after 1935, and food consumption per head was still below 1928 levels into the late 1930s. Strong answers separate the headline industrial growth from the lived experience of Soviet workers.

The Third Plan and the Verdict

The Third Five-Year Plan opened in 1938 with rearmament its overriding priority. Defence spending consumed nearly a third of the state budget by 1940. Civilian projects were squeezed; the Terror had decimated the engineering and managerial cadres just as production quotas rose; output of consumer goods stagnated. The Plan was cut short by Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. By 1941 the USSR was the third largest industrial economy in the world, behind only the United States and Germany. Coal, steel, oil, machine tools and electricity output all dwarfed the 1928 figures. The whole new industrial base east of the Urals was indispensable to the Soviet war effort after 1941. The cost was a generation of suppressed living standards, hundreds of thousands of Gulag deaths in showpiece projects, and a planning system whose distortions endured into the 1980s.

Key Fact

The First Plan (1928–32) built Magnitogorsk, the Dnieper Dam and the Belomor Canal — coal output roughly doubled and pig iron output rose sharply, with Gulag labour central to the showpiece projects. The Second Plan (1933–37) promised the ‘Three Goods’ (food, clothing and housing) but defence spending overrode them after 1935; it also opened the Moscow Metro (1935) and developed industry in the Urals and Siberia. Alexei Stakhanov’s record shift was August 1935; it was used to raise norms across whole industries.
