lessons.title: The Great Terror, the NKVD and the Show Trials

before.content_html:
A Bullet in Leningrad

On 1 December 1934 Sergei Kirov, the popular Leningrad party boss and a member of the Politburo, was shot dead in the corridor of the Smolny Institute by a young party member, Leonid Nikolayev. Stalin took the night train to Leningrad, conducted his own interrogation of the killer, and within days a decree had stripped the accused of the right to defend themselves and ordered their immediate execution. Whether Stalin ordered the murder is still debated — the post-Soviet historian Oleg Khlevniuk concludes there is no archival proof — but its political use is not in doubt. The murder of Kirov became the pretext for the Great Terror, the wave of arrests, executions and Gulag sentences that swept the Soviet Union from 1936 to 1938.

Key Fact

The Soviet secret police was not one fixed body. Genrikh Yagoda ran the NKVD until 1936 and oversaw the first Show Trial; Nikolai Yezhov took over in September 1936 and gave his name to the ‘Yezhovshchina’ of mass arrests in 1937–38; Lavrenti Beria replaced Yezhov in late 1938 and ran the system through the war and into the post-war Gulag.

The Three Moscow Show Trials, 1936–38

The most public face of the Terror was the Moscow Show Trials. In August 1936 Lev Kamenev, Grigory Zinoviev and fourteen other Old Bolsheviks were paraded in the October Hall, accused of plotting Kirov’s murder and of conspiring with the exiled Trotsky to assassinate Stalin. All sixteen confessed; all sixteen were shot. The second trial in January 1937 condemned Yuri Pyatakov and other industrial managers as ‘saboteurs’ and ‘Trotskyite wreckers’. The third in March 1938 broke Nikolai Bukharin, the architect of the NEP and Lenin’s own choice as the party’s ‘valuable theoretician’, who confessed to spying for Germany, Japan and Britain before being shot.

The confessions were not spontaneous. Defendants were beaten, denied sleep, and threatened with the arrest of their wives and children. Some were promised that a confession would save their families; in almost every case the families were arrested anyway. The diplomatic corps and Western journalists were invited to the trials precisely so that they could be reported abroad as proof of the regime’s impartiality. The trials were also retrospective revenge on the men who had defeated Stalin’s rivals in the 1920s — Kamenev and Zinoviev had been Stalin’s allies in 1923–25, Bukharin in 1926–27. The Old Bolshevik generation that had made the October Revolution was being publicly liquidated.

Students sometimes treat the confessions as evidence that the defendants were guilty, or as a free choice to die a Bolshevik death. The archives opened in the 1990s make the coercion plain. Defendants endured the ‘conveyor’ — rotating teams of interrogators questioning the prisoner without sleep for days — and the threat of arrest of their families. Bukharin’s prison letters to Stalin, published after 1991, alternate between protestations of innocence and rehearsed confessions. Strong answers explain that the confessions were a stage-managed performance and weigh both Robert Conquest’s totalitarian reading and Sheila Fitzpatrick’s revisionist insistence that local denouncers and bureaucratic dynamics also drove the process.

The Yezhovshchina, 1937–38

Beneath the public trials ran the deeper terror. From the summer of 1937 NKVD chief Yezhov ran a quota system: each region was assigned a target for arrests in ‘Category 1’ (execution) and ‘Category 2’ (eight to ten years in the camps). NKVD Order 00447 of July 1937 set initial figures of nearly 73,000 to be shot and 186,000 to be camped, but local NKVD chiefs petitioned for higher quotas to prove their zeal, and the totals climbed. The atmosphere was sustained by denunciations: ordinary citizens reporting neighbours, colleagues and even relatives, often to settle private scores or to claim the apartment of a deported family. The historian Sheila Fitzpatrick has shown that denunciation was not only a top-down weapon; ordinary Soviets used it to negotiate the system. Estimates of the dead vary — Conquest’s 1968 figures were higher than the post-1991 archival numbers — but Khlevniuk reckons around 750,000 people were shot in 1937–38 alone, with a further 1.5 million sent to the camps.

Key Fact

NKVD Order 00447, issued in July 1937, formalised the mass operation: regional quotas for ‘Category 1’ (execution) and ‘Category 2’ (eight to ten years in the labour camps), targeting former kulaks, returning émigrés, clergy and ‘anti-Soviet elements’. Local NKVD chiefs routinely petitioned upward to raise their own quotas to demonstrate vigilance.

Purging the Red Army, 1937

In June 1937 Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, the most accomplished commander in the Red Army and architect of its mechanised deep-battle doctrine, was tried in secret with seven other generals and shot the same night. Over the following eighteen months three of the five Soviet marshals, thirteen of fifteen full generals, fifty of fifty-seven corps commanders, and the majority of the officer corps were arrested or executed. The historian Stephen Kotkin notes that some of the ‘evidence’ against Tukhachevsky was a forgery prepared by German intelligence and fed to Stalin via Czechoslovakia — a plant that Stalin chose to believe. The cost was paid in 1941: when Operation Barbarossa hit, the Red Army was being commanded by hastily promoted survivors with little senior experience, and its early disasters owed much to the purge.

The Gulag System

Those who escaped execution went to the Gulag. The camp system, run by the NKVD’s Main Camp Administration, was vast: by 1939 around 1.6 million prisoners were in camps and labour colonies. Kolyma in the Russian Far East was a winter death-zone where prisoners panned for gold in temperatures of minus forty. Vorkuta in the Arctic produced coal. The White Sea–Baltic Canal had been dug by prisoners between 1931 and 1933; thousands died on it, and it was promptly silted up. The economic logic was as much a fiction as the trials — Gulag labour was inefficient and the prisoners died — but the camps gave a hard edge to every denunciation. The line between citizen and prisoner was a knock at the door.

The Show Trials made the Old Bolsheviks famous victims, but they were a small fraction of the total. Order 00447 targeted former kulaks, clergy, returning émigrés, ethnic minorities and ordinary ‘anti-Soviet elements’. National operations against Soviet Poles, Germans and Koreans accounted for around a third of the executions. Most victims were factory workers, peasants and clerks denounced by neighbours or caught by quota-hungry NKVD officers. Strong answers move beyond the famous defendants to the wider sweep of the Yezhovshchina, and engage with the post-Soviet archival school (Khlevniuk) on numbers as well as the older totalitarian school (Conquest) on intent.

Beria, the End of the Yezhovshchina, and 1941

By the autumn of 1938 the Terror had become unmanageable: factories were missing managers, ministries had been thinned out, and the NKVD itself was riddled with arrests as Yezhov turned on his own subordinates. In November 1938 Stalin replaced Yezhov with Lavrenti Beria. Yezhov was quietly arrested, tried in secret and shot in 1940. The mass quotas were dropped, some camp sentences were reviewed, and the regime presented a partial ‘return to normality’ while keeping the Gulag system intact. The Terror had killed roughly three quarters of a million Soviet citizens, broken every potential alternative leadership, and left Stalin’s personal authority absolute on the eve of the German invasion of June 1941. The cost — in officer corps, in technical experts, in social trust — would shape Soviet performance throughout the early stages of the Second World War.

lessons.title: Propaganda, the Cult of Stalin and the 1936 Constitution

before.content_html:
Engineers of Human Souls

In October 1932 Stalin met a group of writers at the Moscow flat of Maxim Gorky and told them that the writer was the ‘engineer of the human soul’. Two years later the First Soviet Writers’ Congress, opened by Gorky and shaped by the cultural commissar Andrei Zhdanov, made Socialist Realism the only permitted style in literature, painting, cinema and music. Earlier independent artistic associations had been dissolved by decree in April 1932; from 1934 a single state-controlled Union of Soviet Writers held the membership cards, the journal contracts and the foreign travel passports. The point was not just to censor opposition but to enlist culture for the regime: paintings of smiling collective farmers, novels of Stakhanovite shock-workers, and films of the October Revolution rewritten with Stalin at Lenin’s shoulder.

Key Fact

Socialist Realism was declared the official doctrine of Soviet art at the First Soviet Writers’ Congress in 1934. Maxim Gorky was its public figurehead; Andrei Zhdanov delivered the keynote that bound writers to portraying socialist construction in optimistic, accessible style. Independent artistic associations had already been dissolved by the April 1932 decree.

Press, Cinema and the Banned Modernists

The press was wholly state-owned. Pravda (‘Truth’) was the Communist Party paper; Izvestia (‘News’) the government’s daily; the press agency TASS supplied every other title. Glavlit, the central censorship agency, vetted every printed word; references to purged figures had to be physically inked out of library books or the books pulped. Cinema was equally policed. Sergei Eisenstein’s October (1928) had already shaped the popular memory of the Bolshevik seizure of power; through the 1930s film studios produced biopics of Lenin and a stream of musical comedies (Volga-Volga, 1938, was reportedly Stalin’s favourite). Modernist composers and painters fared worse: Dmitri Shostakovich’s opera Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk was denounced in Pravda in January 1936 under the headline ‘Muddle Instead of Music’, and the avant-garde tradition of the early 1920s was pushed underground or into exile.

Education, Komsomol and the Rewritten Past

School textbooks were rewritten across the 1930s to give Stalin a starring role in the October Revolution and the Civil War, and to demote or erase Trotsky, Bukharin, Zinoviev and Kamenev as they fell. From 1934 a single official history textbook was prescribed for every Soviet school. Children joined the Young Pioneers (ages 9–14) at scarlet-tie ceremonies; teenagers progressed to the Komsomol at fourteen, where they were trained as activists, sent to construction sites, and screened for full party membership. The cultural campaign was matched by an antireligious one: Stalin’s ‘Godless Five-Year Plan’ from 1932 closed the great majority of Russian Orthodox parishes, arrested or shot priests, and tried to replace Christian festivals with Soviet ones. By 1939 only a few hundred parish churches still functioned in a country that had had over fifty thousand in 1914. The League of the Militant Godless ran the campaign in classrooms and on the streets.

Students often picture artists writing reluctantly under threat. The picture is more complicated. Many writers and film-makers genuinely believed in the socialist project — Gorky and Eisenstein among them. The tightening was incremental: the 1932 decree dissolving independent associations preceded the 1934 Congress; the Shostakovich denunciation came only in 1936. Sheila Fitzpatrick has argued that Soviet artists negotiated the system, choosing genres and subjects that fit official taste while preserving private craft. Strong answers separate the early enthusiasm from the late-1930s coercion and avoid the lazy ‘all artists were forced’ framing.

The 1936 Stalin Constitution

In December 1936 the Eighth Congress of Soviets adopted the new Soviet Constitution, which Stalin had personally chaired the drafting commission for. On paper, it looked like the most progressive document in the world. It guaranteed universal direct suffrage by secret ballot — for the first time including former ‘non-citizens’ such as priests and former kulaks. It promised freedom of speech, press, assembly, religious worship and the inviolability of the home. It listed the rights to work, rest, healthcare, education and old-age provision. Eleven Union Republics were named, each in theory entitled to secede from the USSR.

The reality was the Yezhovshchina. The same year the constitution was adopted, Order 00447 was being drafted, the first Moscow Show Trial had condemned Zinoviev and Kamenev, and arrest quotas were rising. Article 126 of the Constitution declared the Communist Party ‘the leading core of all organisations of the working people, both public and state’ — in practice only the Party could nominate candidates for election, and elections offered a single-name ballot. The Constitution was, in Robert Conquest’s phrase, ‘a paper democracy’: it served as evidence to foreign sympathisers that the USSR was the most democratic state on earth even as the secret police were knocking on doors. Soviet diplomacy used the document, translated into a dozen languages, to recruit Western Popular Front allies and Spanish Republican sympathy in 1937.

Key Fact

The 1936 ‘Stalin Constitution’ was adopted by the Eighth Congress of Soviets in December 1936. It promised universal direct suffrage, freedom of speech, press, assembly and religion, and rights to work, rest and education. Article 126 made the Communist Party the ‘leading core’ of all organisations, and only Party-approved candidates could be nominated — making it a paper democracy during the very year the Yezhovshchina was being prepared.

The Cult of Stalin

Above the press, the cinema and the constitution rose the Cult of Stalin. It built on the existing Lenin cult of 1924: the embalmed body in the Mausoleum, the renaming of Petrograd to Leningrad, the speeches that opened with a Lenin quotation. From his fiftieth birthday in December 1929 Stalin grafted himself on as Lenin’s true heir. By the mid-1930s portraits of Stalin hung in every classroom and factory; statues of Stalin stood in every town square; Stalingrad, Stalinsk, Stalinabad, Stalino and Stalin Peak appeared on the map; the Volga–Don and Moscow–Volga canals carried his name. Newspapers addressed him as ‘Wise Father’ and ‘Beloved Leader of Peoples’. Soviet doctored photographs are the most famous artefact of the cult: Trotsky was airbrushed out of images of Lenin’s 1920 speeches; Yezhov, after his fall in 1938, was edited out of the famous photograph of Stalin walking along the Moscow–Volga Canal.

Students often present the Cult of Stalin as Stalin’s personal invention from scratch. The Lenin cult, with its Mausoleum, Lenin Corners and embalmed body, was already the model. Stalin’s achievement was to graft his own image onto an existing devotional infrastructure and to make himself look like the only authentic Leninist after the Old Bolsheviks had been shot. The historian Stephen Kotkin argues that the cult also met a real demand from below — ordinary Soviets, after years of upheaval, wanted a strong, fatherly leader. Strong answers explain why the regime needed the cult after the Show Trials had killed the men who had actually made the October Revolution.

Why the Cult Mattered

The Cult of Stalin was not decoration. It performed three concrete functions. First, it concentrated authority. After the Show Trials had publicly killed Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin, the cult presented Stalin as the only legitimate heir of October — there were no rivals left because there had never been any. Second, it stabilised a society in violent flux: collectivisation, industrialisation, mass deportations and the Terror were all happening in the same decade, and the image of the Wise Father held the package together as a single national project. Third, it served foreign policy: the smiling, paternal Stalin of the constitution and the cult was the face the Soviet Union showed to the Comintern, to Spanish Republicans and to anti-fascist intellectuals abroad. By 1941 the Stalin who took the salute on the Lenin Mausoleum on the eve of the German invasion was a living icon — one whose first reaction to Barbarossa, on 22 June, was to fall silent for ten days.

lessons.title: Life in Stalin's USSR by 1941: Workers, Women and Minorities

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Urban Soviets in the 1930s lived in kommunalka flats with shared kitchens, queued for rationed bread, and were tied to their cities by internal passports introduced in 1932; the 1940 labour law made unauthorised absence from work a criminal offence.
  • Soviet women entered industry and the professions on a scale unmatched elsewhere — around three quarters of doctors by 1940 — but the 1936 Family Code banned abortion, made divorce harder, and reversed the early Bolshevik record set under Alexandra Kollontai.
  • Ethnic persecution was not just a wartime measure: the Soviet Koreans were deported in 1937, the ‘national operations’ of 1937–38 targeted Poles, Germans and other diaspora communities, and around 440,000 Volga Germans were deported following the German invasion in 1941.
before.content_html:
A Society in Motion

By 1941 the Soviet Union was a country whose social map had been redrawn in fifteen years. Twenty-nine million peasants had moved into the cities to work in the new factories of the First and Second Five-Year Plans. The countryside had been collectivised, dekulakised and partly starved. Women were doing factory and tractor work that would have been unimaginable in 1917. The state had begun deporting whole nationalities. The experience of Soviet life in 1941 depended sharply on who you were: a Stakhanovite shock-worker in the Donbas lived a different life from a kolkhoz peasant in Ukraine or a Soviet Korean being put on a train for Central Asia.

Towns: Kommunalka Flats, Rationing and the Internal Passport

The headline of urban life in the 1930s was housing shortage. Rapid industrialisation drew millions into cities that had not been rebuilt for them; the typical Soviet family lived in a kommunalka — a communal flat in which two or three families shared a kitchen, bathroom and corridor. Food was rationed from 1929 to 1935. Bread was the staple; meat and butter were luxuries; queues for everything were normal. From December 1932 every Soviet citizen aged sixteen or over needed an internal passport with a residence stamp; collective-farm peasants were initially denied passports altogether, which tied them to the kolkhoz like serfs. Factories used piece rates, fines for absenteeism, and from 1932 a labour book recording every job change. The 1940 labour law made unauthorised absence from work a criminal offence punishable by prison.

Key Fact

Internal passports were introduced in December 1932; collective-farm peasants were initially denied them, tying them to the kolkhoz. Bread rationing ran from 1929 to 1935. The 1940 labour law made unauthorised absence from work a criminal offence punishable by prison, alongside piece rates, labour books and fines for lateness.

The Stakhanovites and the Bureaucratic Elite

Soviet life was not uniformly miserable. From August 1935, when the Donbas miner Alexei Stakhanov reportedly cut 102 tonnes of coal in a single shift — fourteen times the norm — the regime promoted the Stakhanovites as a model. Top performers were rewarded with cash bonuses, larger flats with their own kitchens, holiday vouchers to Black Sea sanatoria, and access to closed shops stocked with goods unavailable to ordinary workers. Party officials, NKVD officers and senior managers shared this privileged tier. The historian Sheila Fitzpatrick has described 1930s Soviet society as one of sharp inequality dressed in egalitarian language. The same shop-window that displayed shock-worker rewards also fixed production norms higher across whole sectors, so the unintended cost of the Stakhanovite movement was that ordinary workers had to run faster to meet the new targets.

The Countryside: Kolkhoz Life and the Private Plot

In the countryside the dominant institution was the kolkhoz. Peasants pooled land, livestock and labour and were paid a share of what was left after the state had taken its quota, valued in ‘labour-day’ units that were often worthless. Their lifeline was the small private plot, half a hectare or less, on which they could grow vegetables and keep a cow or pigs — by the late 1930s these private plots produced the majority of urban meat, dairy and eggs despite being a tiny fraction of cultivated land. State farms (sovkhozy) were less common but better paid, with workers on a wage. Rural living standards remained well below urban levels; the houses were wooden, electricity was rare, and the famine of 1932–33 had killed several million people in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and the North Caucasus. From 1935 collective-farm peasants were required to deliver compulsory grain quotas; failure was punishable as ‘sabotage’.

Students often write that everyone in 1930s USSR was equally poor and oppressed. The picture is more textured. Stakhanovites, party bureaucrats, NKVD officers and skilled workers in defence industries lived a recognisably middle-class life with bonuses, larger flats and access to closed shops. Newly literate peasant migrants who had reached the cities and learned a trade saw real upward mobility. The historian Sheila Fitzpatrick has called the 1930s a period of ‘Big Deal’ social bargaining for those who proved useful to the regime. Strong answers explain that experience varied by class, region and ethnicity, and avoid ‘everyone suffered equally’ framing.

Women: Industry, Education and the 1936 Family Code

Soviet women entered industry on a scale unmatched in any other major economy. Between 1928 and 1940 around ten million women joined the urban workforce. Women trained as engineers, doctors and tractor drivers; by 1940 around three quarters of Soviet doctors were women. Education for girls was free and compulsory through to 14, and Soviet propaganda celebrated the model peasant girl who became a tractor driver or a Hero of Socialist Labour. Yet from 1936 the regime sharply rolled back the early Bolshevik record on the family. The 1936 Family Code banned abortion (which had been legalised in 1920 by Alexandra Kollontai’s Commissariat for Social Welfare), made divorce far more expensive and bureaucratic, restored awards for mothers of large families and criminalised male non-payment of child support. Stalin called the family ‘the basic cell of socialist society’. The retrenchment was both ideological — positioning the regime as morally conservative on the eve of war — and demographic: the famines, the Terror, the urban housing crisis and falling birth rates had all reduced the population.

Key Fact

The 1936 Family Code banned abortion (legalised 1920), made divorce expensive and bureaucratic, restored awards for mothers of large families, and criminalised male non-payment of child support. The early-1920s Bolshevik record under Alexandra Kollontai — legal abortion, easy divorce, civil marriage — was sharply reversed. By 1940 around three quarters of Soviet doctors were women, but their position at home had been re-traditionalised.

Persecution of Ethnic Minorities

In August–October 1937 the NKVD deported around 172,000 Soviet Koreans from the Pacific Far East to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, on the grounds that some might spy for Imperial Japan. Around 40,000 are estimated to have died of disease, hunger and cold during or shortly after the journey. Through 1937–38 the ‘national operations’ targeted Soviet Poles, Germans, Latvians, Estonians, Finns, Greeks and Bulgarians; around 350,000 people were arrested and roughly two thirds were shot. After the German invasion in June 1941, Stalin ordered the deportation of around 440,000 Volga Germans — an autonomous community since the eighteenth century — to Siberia and Kazakhstan. The wartime deportations of Crimean Tatars, Chechens, Ingush and Kalmyks would follow in 1943–44, but the Soviet pattern of preventive ethnic deportation began in 1937, well before Operation Barbarossa.

Students often present ethnic deportation as a 1941–44 wartime measure. The Soviet Korean deportation of 1937 came four years before Barbarossa, and the ‘national operations’ of 1937–38 against Poles, Germans and other diaspora communities were running alongside the Yezhovshchina. Lynne Viola and Lynne Lawrence’s work on the special-settlement archives shows preventive ethnic targeting was a 1930s pattern that the war intensified. Strong answers separate pre-war ethnic persecution from wartime deportations and avoid the simpler ‘Stalin reacted to the German invasion’ framing.

The USSR in June 1941

By June 1941, on the eve of Operation Barbarossa, Soviet life had been remade. An urban industrial workforce had been built; women were a majority of doctors and a large minority of engineers; literacy had risen sharply; the Communist Party reached into every workplace through the Komsomol and the Stakhanovite movement. The cost was real and unevenly distributed. Peasants were tied to the kolkhoz with passport controls; workers faced criminal sanctions for absenteeism; women had gained access to industry and lost ground at home; entire ethnic communities had been deported. Stakhanovites and party bureaucrats lived above the rationed economy in a world of bonuses and closed shops. The regime that the German army was about to attack was not the egalitarian society its propaganda described, but it was a Soviet society fundamentally different from the one Lenin had inherited in 1917.

Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of the 1936 Family Code (abortion banned, divorce made expensive, awards for mothers of large families, criminalised non-payment of child support) and the early Bolshevik record under Kollontai (legal abortion 1920, easy divorce, civil marriage) — weighed against the genuine gains made by Soviet women in industry and the professions (around three quarters of doctors female by 1940, ten million women joining the urban workforce 1928–40). Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge in patches; the judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay and barely engages with the interpretations as views. [1–4]

How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 that the persecution of ethnic minorities in the USSR was a long-running pre-war policy rather than a wartime emergency?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
(In addition, 4 marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained evaluation of both interpretations as views, with sharp cross-referencing. Uses precise own knowledge — the deportation of around 172,000 Soviet Koreans in 1937 with Japan as the named threat; the ‘national operations’ of 1937–38 against Poles, Germans, Latvians, Estonians, Finns and Greeks; around 350,000 arrested and roughly two thirds shot — weighed against the wartime evidence (the 440,000 Volga Germans deported after Barbarossa in 1941; the 1943–44 deportation of Crimean Tatars, Chechens, Ingush and Kalmyks). Reaches a clearly justified judgement. SPaG: consistently accurate, with confident use of period vocabulary (NKVD, kolkhoz, internal passport, special settlement, autonomous republic). [16–20 + up to 4 SPaG]
Secure: Both interpretations reviewed; relevant own knowledge applied; judgement made but reasoning at points implicit. SPaG: mostly accurate. [11–15 + 2–3 SPaG]
Developing: Engages with both interpretations unevenly; own knowledge thin or generic; judgement asserted not argued. SPaG: errors that occasionally hinder meaning. [6–10 + 1–2 SPaG]
Emerging: Describes one interpretation; little engagement with the other; little own knowledge. SPaG: frequent errors. [1–5 + 0–1 SPaG]
